pages.text: Here, at the very middle of the Middle Kingdom, is the Beijing you came to see: Chairman Mao slum bering in his mausoleum at the heart of Tianan men Sq, while the ghosts of emperors past haunt the 9999 rooms of the world's largest palace complex, the Forbidden City. Remarkably, central Beijing retains its historic, lowslung layout, a fantastical masterwork of feng shui planning and divine order. You'll understand as soon as you clamber up the slopes of Jingshan Park and drink in the astonishing scale and symmetry of the city's Central Axis from above. Ideally, you'll dedicate one or two days to the main sights, but consider getting off the beaten path with a trip to lesser-known museums and parks. Chang'an Jie, Beijing's grand east-west central ave nue used for military parades, divides the Forbidden City from Tiananmen Sq, and Wangfujing from the for mer Legation Quarter (currently closed to the public). Hidden in between (p70 ) and the Tiananmen Sq Forbidden (p72 ) are two havens of shaded park space: the City Workers' Cultural Palace ( , Láodòng Rénmín Wénhuà Gōng) to the east and Zhongshan Park to the west. pages.text: The rectangular arrangement of Tiananmen Sq, its many red flags rippling in the wind, to some extent pays obeisance to traditional Chinese culture, but most of its ornaments and buildings are Soviet-inspired. Mao conceived the square to project the power of the Communist Party, and during the Cultural Revolution he reviewed parades of up to a million people here. pages.text: Although you can explore the Forbidden City in a few hours, a full day will keep you occupied - it is a truly colossal place. Much like the Louvre, you can't see it all at once, so focus on the parts that grab your attention. Many visitors get caught up with the vast ceremonial halls and parade grounds of the Outer Court (southern half), but remember that the real thrill comes from exploring the : the labyrinth Inner Court of courtyards and halls north of the Outer Court, laid out on a more human scale. Be prepared to walk long distances. The Forbidden City was renamed the Palace Museum ( , Gùgōng Bówùguǎn) in 1925, just one year after Puyi, the abdicated last emperor, departed the Inner Court.

The Outer Court is dominated by the Three Great Halls set in vast cobbled courtyards, which could hold thousands of dig nitaries and their sedan-chair bearers, guards and servants. The is the most important and Hall of Supreme Harmony largest structure in the Forbidden City. It was used for state occasions, such as the emperor’s birthday, coronations and the nomination of military leaders. Inside the hall is a richly deco rated Dragon Throne, from which the emperor would preside over trembling officials. Behind the Hall of Supreme Harmony is the square Hall of , which was used as the emperor’s transit Central Harmony lounge. Here he would make last-minute preparations, rehearse speeches and receive ministers. Begin by dipping two or three slices of meat into the fermented bean sauce, then place the slices at the top of the wrapper. Add some julienned cucumbers and spring onions on top of this, and perhaps some pickled veggies and garlic sauce while you're at it. Fold the wrapper in half (a semicir cle), and then fold in the sides so nothing leaks out. Voila! You're ready to enjoy the ultimate Beijing meal. pages.text: A pilgrimage to the Temple of Heaven, 3km south of the Forbidden City, is as mandatory for tourists today as it was for emperors and their entourages coming here during the winter solstice to pay tribute to the gods. The temple and its surrounding park occupies a vast tranche of real estate - prepare for a lot of walking. During the Ming and Qing dynasties, the grounds were off limits to all but the emperor and his ministers, and only used for occasional ceremonies. You'll also find enticing remnants of Beijing's city walls north of the temple, where a walking route ex tends eastwards for 1.2km alongside a wistful stretch of worn brick and stone. Historians will want to make a beeline for the new home of the imperial archives, once stored next to the Forbidden City. Immediately south of Tiananmen Sq is Qianmen Dajie, conveying tourists along Beijing's Central Axis. A conduit to the cosmos, the ( , Tiāntán; Temple of Heaven Tiantan Donglu, ) originally served as the vast stage for solemn rites performed by the emperor, who prayed here twice a year for good harvests and divine atonement. Now a vast park dotted with 4000 cypress trees, the tem ple is known for its Long Corridor and th

a storeroom, used for the divine spirit tablets and other sacri ficial materials. The Echo Wall, 65m in diameter, is so named for its unique acoustic properties. A quiet word or two spo ken a few feet from the wall can be heard at the opposite point on the circle. The sacrifices themselves were made at the , Round Altar a raised dais open to the elements at the southern end of the axis. Arranged in three tiers, its divine geometry revolves around the imperial number nine, considered sacrosanct in imperial China. Book tickets in advance at forbiddencitytickets.com. The main entrance is the east gate (Subway Line 5); the closest place to eat is the Hongqiao Pearl Market (p 90 ).

pages.text: Like all ancient Chinese capitals, Beijing was origi nally divided into an Inner City and Outer City, and it was at Qianmen - the Front Gate - that these two worlds met. Just beyond Qianmen was the busy com mercial district of Dashilar ( , Dàzhàlánr), filled with craftspeople, peddlers and an endless pro cession of travellers. Dashilar was also an entertain ment district that was known for its theatres and more illicit pleasures, a tradition that continued all the way up to the communist era. Today, the shopping streets of Dashilar and near by Liulichang are the best areas for browsing tradi tional Chinese goods like silk and tea, or catching a performance of Peking opera. Further afield are the city's Ancient Architecture Museum and the Niujie Mosque. Delve into the smaller alleys flowing west from Meishi Jie - like Yangmeizhu Xiejie, a former printing street once home to author Lu Xun - for the most authentic local vibes. The capital's best purveyor of history tours in English, Beijing (bjpostcards.com; 97 Yangmeizhu Xiejie, Postcards 97 ) hosts a range of rigorously researched walks led by Danish cofounder Lars. pages.text: Experts insist that there was never a ‘Great Wall of China’, but rather - many walls that were woven together over time. The surviving segments in Hebei province are scattered across the northern highlands, some connected to each other, others isolated. For lovers of history and architecture, each site represents a unique state of repair (or disrepair), as well as a diff erent era in the evolution of Chinese defence. So many stairs and watchtowers can get repetitive after awhile, yet these locations show off the dynamism and adaptability of the Great Wall, and the many ways it has survived the centuries. In some cases, the eff ects of neglect are as striking as the power of restoration. ( , Sīmǎtái), in Miyun district ( , Mìyún Simatai Qū), has won global attention for its mountain scenery, which is epic even by Great Wall standards. Restorers have used a lighter touch on these 10 watchtowers and the walls that join them. Much of the original stonework is still visible, lending Simatai a more authentic feel than its fl ashier cousins. But it is far more than that. Much of the New Territories is designated as country parks or protected areas - a hiking paradise with trails that take in rugged mountains, bizarre rock formations and whitesand beaches. Elsewhere, ancient walled towns and forgotten fishing villages render its name a misnomer. In the west of Lantau, the Tanka village of Tai O deserves the moniker ‘unspoiled’ - it’s as close as you are going to get to an authentic fishing community in Hong Kong. The Tanka peo ple who founded Tai O built houses on stilts above the tidal flats when they first moved to the area, and that way of life has been preserved centuries later. For the best view of the Stilt Houses , look east from Sun Ki Bridge or take one of the numerous boat tours that depart from near the bridge. pages.text: No trip to Hong Kong is complete without visiting Ngong Ping plateau for the seated Tian Tan Buddha statue. The statue, a giant, 26.4m-high representation of Lord Gautama, sits at the top of a 268-step staircase. The statue itself weighs in at a whopping 250 tonnes and is made from 202 separate bronze pieces, and can be seen aerially as you fly into Hong Kong, or on a clear day from Macau.

Home of the stock exchange, corporate high-rises, and world-class restaurants, bars and shopping, ‘Central’ is a work-hard, playhard metropolis that never lets up. The promise of quick riches has attracted opportunists of all stripes here since the days when Hong Kong was named Victoria, Great Britain’s colonial-era entrepot. Skyscrapers might have superseded shipping warehouses, but Central remains a workaholic, profit-driven pleasure hub. It’s not all mirrored glass and Prada, of course. In the shadow of all those high-rises lurks an appealing workaday Central of family-run noodle shops, outdoor markets and fading pockets of heritage. And while tourist attractions are relatively few, the appeal of Central has always been its energy (subdued though it is since the pro-democracy crackdown) in the whirl of commerce, the pounding of jackhammers and the sense of opportunity that’s there for the taking. pages.text: Around an hour west of Hong Kong - whether you go by hydrofoil ferry or across the monumental Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge - Macau is one of China’s Special Administrative Regions with its own government, currency and colonial legacy. Once a Portuguese colony from the middle of the 16th century until 1999, when it was handed back to China, it’s now it’s a dazzling casino enclave that gives Vegas a run for its money. But away from the glitz, the old Portuguese-Chinese hybridity endures. Strolling through the old, UNESCO-listed city centre, you can snack on pastéis de nata and gaze up at the the iconic Church of St Paul. Cast in photogenic ruins, it was constructed by Jesuit missionaries who built a rapport with China’s emperors through intellectual exchange, map-making and engaging with Chinese culture. Built in the 17th century, was once a defensive Monte Fort stronghold used to protect the burgeoning colony from pirates and invaders. Today, it offers a glimpse into Macau’s colonial past with its well-preserved battlements and historic cannons. Barracks and storehouses were designed to allow the fort to survive a two-year siege, but the cannons were fired only once - during the aborted attempt by the Dutch to invade Macau in 1622. From the fort’s summit you can gaze out over major Macau’s landmarks, including the Ruins of the Church of St Paul, the Guia Lighthouse (part of the Guia Fortress & Chapel; p534), the architecturally distinctive Grand Lisboa, the Macau Tower (p534) and the modern skyscrapers of Portas do Cerco.

pages.text: 'You are a Shenzhener once you come here', is the city slogan of Shenzhen ( , Shēnzhèn), a nod to its migrant culture and inclusive attitude. Bordering Hong Kong, Shenzhen began its rise to fame in the 1980s, when it was chosen as the first of China’s Special Economic Zones, areas that experimented with capitalistic policies and attracted foreign investment. Shenzhen was the place where Chinese nationals could realise their dreams of financial success, even if they came from poor farming families. Upward mobility came in the form of selling from a 1m counter in the Huaxiangbei area (the world’s largest electronics market) then eventually becoming insanely rich;-the exact trajectory of several of Shenzhen’s 50,300 millionaires. Today, Shenzhen's known as the 'Silicon Valley' of China, with tech giants Tencent and Huawei headquartered here. However, to understand its past and present, lies in its urban villages - especially in what gets destroyed and what gets preserved. pages.text: Guangzhou ( , Guǎngzhōu) has always been a liminal space between China and the rest of the world. Built up on either side of the Pearl River, it was the starting point of the Maritime Silk Road and China’s busiest port of trade for hundreds of years. Attracting both entrepreneurs and revolutionaries has made it a dynamic city, and its hodgepodge of cultures can be felt in its diverse restaurants as much as in the languages spoken on its streets. Today, it’s China’s third-largest city, and host of the Canton Fair, a semi-annual trade fair where exporters and importers discuss deals over displays of products showcasing the latest in Chinese innovation. However, the pace of life here is calmer than that of China’s northern metropolises, and given the plethora of historic sites, temples and museums, it's one of the area's best places to learn about the history of the Lingnan region. If anything ails you, the cure can probably be found at ( , Qīngpíng Qingping Chinese Medicine Market Shìchǎng; 23-25 Zhuji Lu, 23-25 ) in one of its more than 1200 stalls. pages.text: Before Guangzhou was Canton, it was Panyu, the capital of the Nanye kingdom - encompassing modern-day South China and parts of Vietnam. Nanyue’s second king, Zhao Mo, declared himself emperor (not just king) of Nanyue in rebellion against the Han dynasty who viewed Nanyue as a vassal state. The ( , Nányuèwáng Mausoleum of the Nanyue King Mù) is where he was buried in 122 BCE with treasures, 15 sac rificial servants and concubines - one of whose skeletal re mains are encased in glass inside the crypt’s seven chambers. For only ¥10 you can enter the red quartz sandstone structure and descend the steps into the crypt at the back of the complex. Afterwards, go to the exhibit hall above to see the excavated treasures, like Zhao Mo’s burial shroud of 2291 jade pieces, and official seals made of jade, gold, turquoise and agate. Other items among the 1000 pieces buried with him include crossbows and fish percussion instruments. Display descriptions are in English and Chinese. Before you leave, swing by the front exhibit hall to check out the display of beautiful but uncomfortable-looking porcelain pillows from the Ming and Qing dynasties. pages.heads: Chaozhou
pages.subs: See the Moveable · Guangji Bridge
pages.text: To the east of Guangzhou lie the lands of very adaptable peoples that immigrated from central China ages ago, the Teochew and the Hakka. The Teochew developed the gōngfū tea ceremony to improve lower-quality tea, and the Hakka built massive clan homes - coiled dragon houses and tǔlóu - for living and protection. Experience a gōngfū tea ceremony in Chaozhou, and see the ingeniously designed Guangji Bridge. The Hakka compounds can be found on the outskirts of Meizhou, about 150km north of Chaozhou. Southwest of Meizhou, just north of Guangzhou, is the small rockclimbing hub of Yingxi in Qingyuan, famous more for its free-range chickens than its peoples. In ( , Cháozhōu), the ( Chaozhou Guangji Bridge , Guǎngjǐ Qiáo) is a ponton bridge made up of 18 boats and 24 stone pagodas. It opens and closes each day - just as it has done for hundreds of years. Originally built in 1171, it straddles the Han River and was one of ancient China’s four famous bridges. Formerly made of stone arches at its ends and 86 boats strung together in the middle, it was likely the fi rst open-close bridge in the world. The bridge acted as an important trade passageway, connecting the south with the rest of Chin

For rock climbing in South China, it’s a great alternative to Yangshuo for those seeking less-crowded peaks and more rural environs. Routes here range from 5.9 to 5.13. While it’s possible to bring your own gear to climb here, you can also rent equipment from Bobo, the owner of Mental Rock (p604), a climbing cafe and guesthouse with a bouldering wall. Expect a bit of hiking to reach the crag (possibly past unsuspecting cows), as well as views of green karst countryside from the top.
